[PATH:empirical] Comparative transcriptomic and metabolic imaging studies across species with varying synaptic densities (e.g., rodents, primates, cetaceans) to quantify ATP consumption per synapse and whole-brain metabolic rate as a function of synaptic density. — Directly tests the predicted transition from sublinear to superlinear metabolic scaling by measuring actual metabolic cost across a range of synaptic densities in intact neural systems.

[PATH:theoretical] Computational modeling of energy-efficient neural scaling using integrate-and-fire networks with tunable synaptic density, incorporating realistic biophysical constraints (e.g., mitochondrial capacity, vesicle recycling limits). — Allows controlled exploration of the hypothesized threshold and the mechanisms that could cause the shift to superlinear cost scaling, providing mechanistic predictions for empirical tests.

[PATH:literature] Systematic re-analysis of existing datasets on brain metabolic rate (e.g., positron emission tomography, 2-deoxyglucose autoradiography) and synaptic density estimates (e.g., from stereological or immunohistological studies) across multiple mammalian species. — Leverages published but possibly unconnected data to evaluate whether the scaling relationship holds across taxa and whether a threshold synaptic density is consistently associated with a change in scaling exponent.

qualifier.geographic: global (studied across multiple species and laboratories)

evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: biological neural systems with high complexity linear or superlinear scaling of metabolic cost with neural complexity, potentially due to increased processing demands and synaptic connectivity]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative allometric analysis of metabolic rates (e.g., glucose uptake via 2-deoxyglucose or fMRI-BOLD) across species with varying brain complexity, controlling for body size and phylogeny — Directly tests whether metabolic cost scales linearly or superlinearly with neural complexity (e.g., number of neurons, synaptic density) in biological systems, providing quantitative data to confirm or refute the hypothesized scaling relationship.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of neural network energy efficiency using biophysically realistic spiking neuron models (e.g., Hodgkin-Huxley or Izhikevich models) with varying connectivity densities and firing rates — Simulates the metabolic cost of processing demands and synaptic connectivity in silico, allowing controlled tests of whether complexity drives superlinear energy scaling under realistic constraints, independent of confounding biological variables.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on brain metabolism and neural complexity (e.g., studies on cortical folding, synaptic density, or neuron counts in relation to oxygen/glucose consumption across vertebrates) — Synthesizes available empirical data from diverse species and studies to assess the generality and slope of the metabolic cost–complexity relationship, identifying gaps or inconsistencies that could challenge the hypothesis.

C007.subject: current deep learning models
C007.object: sublinear scaling of metabolic cost with neural complexity when trained with biologically plausible local learning rules instead of backpropagation
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: current deep learning models sublinear scaling of metabolic cost with neural complexity when trained with biologically plausible local learning rules instead of backpropagation]

[PATH:empirical] Comparative scaling experiments on deep learning models (e.g., ResNet, Transformer) trained with local learning rules (e.g., forward-forward, Hebbian, or contrastive Hebbian) vs. backpropagation, measuring total energy consumption (FLOPs + memory access) per parameter across varying model sizes. — Directly tests the sublinear scaling claim by quantifying metabolic cost (energy) as a function of neural complexity (parameter count) under biologically plausible vs. standard training, controlling for architecture and dataset.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of computational complexity for local learning rules (e.g., weight transport, feedback alignment, or local contrastive objectives) compared to backpropagation, focusing on per-layer update cost and total gradient estimation cost as a function of network depth and width. — Provides an analytical bound on whether local rules inherently reduce the scaling exponent of energy with respect to complexity, independent of implementation details, thus confirming or refuting the hypothesis in principle.

[PATH:literature] Literature survey of recent papers (2020–2025) reporting energy or computational cost scaling in neuromorphic or biologically plausible deep learning systems, e.g., from NeurIPS, ICLR, or Nature Machine Intelligence. — Aggregates existing empirical and theoretical evidence to assess consensus and identify whether sublinear scaling has been observed or contradicted across different local learning rule variants and model scales.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative scaling analysis of compute cost vs. parameter count across transformer and MoE architectures (e.g., scaling laws from Kaplan et al., 2020, and subsequent work on sparsely activated models) — Directly tests whether metabolic (compute) cost scales sublinearly, linearly, or superlinearly with neural complexity (parameters) in current models, revealing if efficiency gains beyond biological constraints are achieved.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of information-theoretic bounds on neural network efficiency (e.g., work on the minimum description length principle or neural tangent kernel scaling) — Provides formal bounds on whether deep learning models can avoid superlinear scaling by leveraging architectural inductive biases or optimization dynamics that biological systems do not possess.

[PATH:literature] Literature review of empirical studies comparing metabolic (energy) scaling in biological neural networks vs. artificial networks (e.g., Laughlin et al., 1998, and recent neuromorphic chip benchmarks) — Synthesizes existing evidence to determine if biological constraints impose a superlinear scaling that current deep learning models demonstrably circumvent via alternative optimization objectives or hardware abstractions.
